'''''Zamioculcas''''' is a genus of [[flowering plant]]s in the family [[Araceae]], containing the single species '''''Zamioculcas zamiifolia.'''''<ref name="POWO a">{{Cite web |title=Zamioculcas Schott {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:2950-1 |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> It is a [[tropical]] [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]], and is native to eastern [[Africa]], including [[Kenya]], [[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Malawi]], [[Mozambique]], [[Tanzania]], and [[Zimbabwe]].<ref name="POWO a" /> Its common names include '''Zanzibar gem''', '''Zuzu plant''', '''emerald palm''', '''ZZ plant''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=ZZ Plant |url=https://homegarden.cahnr.uconn.edu/factsheets/zz-plant/ |publisher=[[University of Connecticut]] |access-date=7 April 2026}}</ref> '''aroid palm''' and '''eternity plant'''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.royalgreen.nl/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=120&Itemid=131&lang=en|title=Zamioculcas - EMERALD PALM|last=Administrator|website=www.royalgreen.nl|access-date=2017-05-18|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612143741/http://www.royalgreen.nl/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=120&Itemid=131&lang=en|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is commonly grown as a [[houseplant]], mainly because it has attractive glossy foliage and is easy to care for. ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' is [[Hardiness zones|winter-hardy in USDA Zones 9 and 10]].<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden">{{Cite web |title=''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276468&isprofile=1&basic=ZZ%20plant |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

==Description==
=== Vegetative characteristics ===
It is a terrestrial,<ref name = "SANBI" /> succulent, slowly growing,<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" /> poisonous,<ref name = "Queensland Government" /> evergreen, rhizomatous, perennial<ref name = "RHS">''Zamioculcas zamiifolia''. (n.d.). Royal Horticultural Society. Retrieved January 4, 2026, from https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/19185/wd/details</ref> herb with erect,<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" /> pinnately compound,<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden" /> 40–60 cm long leaves<ref name = "RHS" /> bearing 6–8 leaflet pairs.<ref name = "RHS" /><ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden" /> The petiole is thick.<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" /> It has a large<ref name = "Queensland Government" /> bulbous, fleshy,<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" /> potato-like rhizome.<ref name = "Queensland Government">Queensland Government. (n.d.). Zanzibar gem. Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Retrieved January 4, 2026, from https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/plants-and-mushrooms/zanzibar-gem-zamioculcas-zamiifolia</ref>
=== Generative characteristics ===
The [[flower]]s are produced in a small, bright yellow to brown or bronze [[spadix (botany)|spadix]] {{convert|5–7|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long and wrapped in a yellow-green [[spathe]]. The whole inflorescence is partly hidden among the branch bases. Flowering is from midsummer to early autumn.{{cn|date=January 2026}}

===Chromosome count===
The chromosome count is 2n = 34.<ref name = "Marchant, 1973">Marchant, C. J. (1973). [http://www.aroidsociety.org/gallery/gibernau/1979/Chromosome%20variation%20in%20araceae%20-%20chap%205%20-%20Marchant%201973.pdf Chromosome variation in Araceae: V. Acoreae to Lasieae.] Kew Bulletin, 199-210.</ref><ref name = "Vanzie-Canton & Leonhardt, 2007">Vanzie-Canton, S. D., & Leonhardt, K. W. (2007, June). [https://www.actahort.org/books/813/813_72.htm In vivo polyploidization of ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia''.] In VI International Symposium on New Floricultural Crops 813 (pp. 531-538).</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was first described as ''Caladium zamiifolium'' {{au|G.Lodd.}} by [[Conrad Loddiges]] in 1829.<ref name = "IPNI a">''Caladium zamiifolium'' G.Lodd. (n.d.). International Plant Names Index. Retrieved January 4, 2026, from https://www.ipni.org/n/86441-1</ref> It was placed into a new monotypic genus ''Zamioculcas'' {{au|Schott}}<ref name="POWO a" /> as ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' {{au|(G.Lodd.) Engl.}} by [[Adolf Engler]] in 1905.<ref name = "POWO b">''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' (G.Lodd.) Engl. (n.d.). Plants of the World Online. Retrieved January 4, 2026, from https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:89402-1</ref>
===Etymology===
The genus ''Zamioculcas'' derives its name from the similarity of its foliage to that of the [[cycad]] genus ''[[Zamia]]'' and its kinship to the [[Araceae]] genus ''[[Colocasia]]'', whose name comes from the word {{transliteration|mis|culcas}} or {{transliteration|mis|colcas}} (from an ancient Middle Eastern name),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=107697|title=Colocasia|website=Flora of North America|access-date=August 4, 2018}}</ref> [[Arabic]] ''qolqas'' ({{langx|arz|قلقاس}}, {{IPA|arz|ʔolˈʔæːs|IPA}}), i.e. [[taro]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://egyptian-cuisine-recipes.com/vegetables/colcasia-%D9%82%D9%84%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B3.html|title=Colcasia قلقاس|work=egyptian-cuisine-recipes.com|access-date=August 4, 2018}}.</ref>

The species name ''zamiifolia'' means "leaves like Zamia" and is formed from the botanical name ''Zamia'' and the Latin word [[wiktionary:folium|''folium'']], leaf.<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener">{{Cite web |title=''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' (Aroid Palm, Emerald Palm, Eternity Plant, Zanzibar Gem, Zuzu Plant, ZZ Plant) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/zamioculcas-zamiifolia/ |access-date=2023-10-23 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is native to Kenya, South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe.<ref name = "POWO b" />

==Conservation==
In South Africa, its national conservation status is least concern (LC).<ref name = "SANBI">South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI). (n.d.). ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' (Lodd.) Engl. SANBI Red List of South African Plants. Retrieved January 4, 2026, from https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3625-1</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[Image:Zamioculcas zamiifolia bluete1.jpg|thumb|right|230px|Inflorescence]]
It is cultivated as a houseplant.<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" /> Dutch nurseries began wide-scale commercial propagation of the plant around 1996.<ref>{{cite book |last = Catherine |first = Horwood |title = Potted History: The Story of Plants in the Home |publisher = Frances Lincoln Ltd |page = 173 |year = 2007 |isbn = 978-0-7112-2800-9}}</ref>

=== Temperature ===
It may survive outdoors as long as the temperature does not fall below around {{cvt|15|C|F|round=5}}; though best growth is between {{cvt|18|and|26|C|F}} while high temperatures give an increase in leaf production. In temperate regions, it is grown as a [[houseplant]]. Overwatering may destroy this plant through [[tuber]] rot. Bright, indirect light is best. Some sun will be tolerated.<ref name="Chen">{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Jianjun|last2=Henny|first2=Richard|title=ZZ: A Unique Tropical Ornamental Foliage Plant|journal=HortTechnology|date=September 2003|volume=13|issue=3|pages=458–462|url=http://horttech.ashspublications.org/content/13/3/458.full.pdf+html|access-date=14 March 2016|doi=10.21273/horttech.13.3.0458|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Propagation ===
''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' may be propagated by leaf cuttings: typically, the lower ends of detached leaves are inserted into a moist, gritty growing medium, and the pot is enclosed in a polythene bag. Though the leaves may well decay, succulent bulb-like structures should form in the bag, and these may be potted up to produce new plants. The process may take upwards of one year. The plant can also be propagated by division.

=== Light ===
Due to its strong green leaves, it is especially suitable for open, bright rooms.<ref>L'Ami des Jardins (ed.): Climatic plants in the house: Healthy living with detoxifying houseplants . Bassermann Verlag, Munich 2012, {{ISBN|978-3-641-67900-2}} , p.  20</ref> When grown indoors, the plant prefers bright indirect light but will tolerate low light conditions. However, lower light is not optimal for an extended period of time. Insufficient amounts of sunlight can result in leaves lengthening and/or falling off, yellowing ([[chlorosis]]), and generally uneven or disproportionate growth as the plant stretches towards a light source. When grown outdoors, ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' prefers part shade to full shade.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden" />

=== Soil ===
The substrate used must be well-drained and contain nutrients. It can be composed of a mixture of tanned ox manure, washed river sand and red earth (1:1:1).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Machado |first=Suzana |date=2022-09-25 |title=Zamioculca: 5 dicas para cuidar da "planta da fortuna". |url=https://enfeitedecora.com/planta-zamioculca-na-decoracao/ |access-date=2023-10-04 |language=pt-BR}}</ref> For indoor plants, use a well-drained potting soil mix.<ref name="North Carolina Extension Gardener" />

=== Water ===
''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' contains 91% water in the leaves, and 95% water in the [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]].<ref name="Moullec" /> It has an individual leaf longevity of at least six months, which may be the reason it can survive extremely well under interior low light levels for four months without water.<ref name="Chen"/> ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' roots are [[rhizomatous]] and have the ability to store moisture, thus aiding the plants in their drought resistance. The plants like regular waterings, but the soil should be allowed to dry out between waterings.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden" />

=== Usage in traditional medicine ===
Though little information is available, ''Z. zamiifolia'' is apparently used medicinally in the [[Mulanje]] District of [[Malawi]] and in the [[East Usambara]] mountains of Tanzania where juice from the leaves is used to treat earache.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Beentje|first1=Henk|title=Flora of Tropical East Africa - Araceae (1985)|date=1985|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9061913225|page=15|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3pqD-8DUk_YC&q=S.J.+Mayo,+Flora+of+Tropical+East+Africa,+Araceae,+A.+A.+Balkema,+Rotterdam/Boston,+1985.&pg=PP1}}</ref>

In Tanzania, a poultice of bruised plant material from ''Z. zamiifolia'' is used as a treatment for the inflammatory condition known as "mshipa".<ref name="Watt">{{cite book|last1=Watt|first1=J.M.|last2=Breyer-Brandwijk|first2=M.G.|title=The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa, Being and Account of Their Medicinal and Other Uses, Chemical Composition, Pharmacological Effects and Toxicology in Man and Animal|date=1962|publisher=E. & S. Livingstone Ltd}}</ref>

Roots from ''Z. zamiifolia'' are used as a local application to treat ulceration by the [[Sukuma people]] in north-western Tanzania.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=P.R.O.|first1=Bally|title=Native Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of East Africa|journal=Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information|volume=1937|issue=1|pages=10–26|date=26 October 1937|doi=10.2307/4107637 |jstor=4107637}}</ref>

==Chemistry==

=== Phytochemicals ===
Several compounds have been isolated from ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia''. The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] contain [[rosmarinic acid]], [[protocatechuic aldehyde]], (''E'')-[[caffeic acid]] and (''E'')- and (''Z'')-[[caffeic acid methyl ester]].<ref name="Moullec" /> The rare natural products (3R,4S,5S)-2,3,4,5-tetrahydroxytetrahydro-2 H-pyran-2-carboxylic acid and apigenin 6-''C''-(6″-(3-hydroxy-3-methyl-glutaroyl)-ß-glucopyranoside) occur in the leaves.<ref name="Moullec" />

===Toxicity===
''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' is part of the family [[Araceae]], which is known to contain [[cyanogenic glycosides]], [[calcium oxalate]]s and perhaps [[alkaloid]]s.<ref name="Moullec" /> A toxicological experiment using [[Artemia salina|brine shrimp]] as a lethality assay did not indicate lethality to the shrimp.<ref name="Moullec">{{cite journal|last1=Moullec|first1=Angharad|title=First identification of natural products from the African medicinal plant ''Zamioculcas zamiifolia'' — A drought resistant survivor through millions of years|journal=Fitoterapia|date=October 2015|volume= 106|pages=280–285|doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2015.09.011|pmid=26385196|hdl=1956/17550|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

===Air purification===
A study demonstrated that, in a laboratory setting, the plant is able to remove [[volatile organic compounds]] in the following order of effectiveness: [[benzene]], [[toluene]], [[ethylbenzene]] and [[xylene]] at a molar flux of around 0.01 mol/(m<sup>2</sup> day). The study stated that any effectiveness on indoor environments is inconclusive.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dela Cruz|first1=Majbrit|last2=Christensen|first2=Jan H.|last3=Thomsen|first3=Jane Dyrhauge|last4=Müller|first4=Renate|title=Can ornamental potted plants remove volatile organic compounds from indoor air? — areview|journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research|volume=21|issue=24|pages=13909–13928|date=19 June 2014|doi=10.1007/s11356-014-3240-x|url=https://greenplantsforgreenbuildings.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Dela-Cruz-2014-review-on-phytoremediation-with-indoor-plants-2.pdf|access-date=14 March 2016|pmid=25056742|s2cid=207272189}}</ref>
